articles.title_orig: Will Tom Cruise’s ‘Digger’ Continue Warner Bros.’ Dismal Box Office Year?
articles.title_zh: Will Tom Cruise’s ‘Digger’ Continue Warner Bros.’ Dismal Box Office Year?
articles.content_orig:
Senior Film and Media Reporter
Tom Cruise has built a career on jumping out of airplanes, scaling skyscrapers and performing other high-wire antics in the name of entertainment. His next stunt may be his riskiest yet: Getting moviegoers to see “ Digger ,” a rare big-budget, star-driven R-rated original comedy.
The Warner Bros. release, which opens on Oct. 2, represents one of the fall season’s biggest gambles. There’s pressure on “Digger” not just to offset the studio’s terrible year at the box office (with bombs including Maggie Gyllenhaal’s punk rock “The Bride!” and DC’s “Supergirl”) but also to impress the new corporate ownership. Paramount Skydance hopes to imminently close its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery.
It might not be Digger Rockwell to the rescue. “Digger,” directed by Alejandro González Iñárritu and starring an unrecognizable Cruise as a powerful oil tycoon whose company sparks an ecological calamity, is tracking a hugely disappointing launch of $12 million to $15 million in North America. Projections were at $18 million to $20 million but were revised down in recent days.
The film was greenlit at $125 million, but according to four knowledgable sources, the budget climbed to $160 million to $180 million after production went over schedule. A Warner Bros. spokesperson disputes those figures. Regardless, a movie of this size would need a debut near $40 million to justify its budget, per rival execs. Since exhibitors keep about half of ticket sales, and the studio spent another $100 million on marketing, “Digger” has a theatrical break-even point of roughly $350 million globally, according to executives with knowledge of similar films. A Warner Bros. spokesperson pushed back, saying the film’s break-even point is $300 million.
Reviews and word of mouth will factor into the film’s box office longevity, analysts say. They also note that “Digger” could be bigger overseas, where Cruise’s movies tend to make the bulk of their money. Profitability for WB may take longer because Cruise gets first-dollar gross, meaning he earns a percentage of revenues before the studio recoups any costs.
“Kudos to Warner Bros. for taking a chance; Tom Cruise has earned that right,” says analyst Jeff Bock of Exhibitor Relations. “But let’s be honest about where Tom Cruise is today. He’s a franchise machine. Can audiences accept him as a transformative actor again after he’s branded himself as the action hero?”
“Digger” is Cruise’s first original movie since 2017’s hit “American Made.” (That year, he also starred in the notorious flop “The Mummy.”) A bankable draw since the ‘80s, Cruise became synonymous with action stardom through the enduring “Mission: Impossible” franchise and then endeared himself to younger generations with 2022’s blockbuster “Top Gun: Maverick.” But even Cruise has learned the hard way that moviegoers have become pickier about what’s worth getting off the couch for. His final two “Mission: Impossible” films — 2023’s “Dead Reckoning” and 2025’s “The Final Reckoning” — faced diminishing returns at the box office.
Cruise, an elusive star who doesn’t talk to press, has worked aggressively — if selectively — to sell “Digger.” Amid his global promotional tour, he made a rare podcast appearance on Travis and Jason Kelce’s “New Heights” and sat for his first cover story in two decades with GQ magazine — which raised eyebrows because the actor managed to avoid any personal questions and relentlessly directed the conversation back to his passion for movies.
“It takes a herculean effort to get word-of-mouth going for a black comedy,” says Bock. “Tom knows he has to go the extra mile with this film. His name alone isn’t going to sell it.”
Beyond Cruise’s star power, Warner Bros. co-chairs Pamela Abdy and Michael De Luca were willing to spend big on “Digger” because Iñárritu, too, has a strong commercial track record. His 2015 film “The Revenant” generated $533 million globally and earned Leonardo DiCaprio his long-awaited best actor Oscar. And 2014’s “Birdman” grossed $103 million against an $18 million budget and won best picture. Iñárritu hasn’t released a film theatrically in more than a decade; his last movie, the polarizing drama “Bardo, False Chronicle of a Handful of Truths,” was set at Netflix.
“The combination of an accomplished auteur and a top star has resulted in some very interesting and successful pictures,” says analyst David A. Gross of Franchise Re, citing examples like “One Battle After Another” with DiCaprio and director Paul Thomas Anderson and “F1” with Brad Pitt and director Joseph Kosinski. “But the movie has to connect and satisfy broad tastes. If word-of-mouth is poor, the film is going to struggle.”
Abdy and De Luca, known for their taste and talent relations, faced similar scrutiny ahead of last year’s “One Battle After Another” — another expensive, auteurist swing. That film opened to $22 million and climbed to $213 million globally. Although an impressive result for a nearly three-hour original comedic drama, those returns weren’t enough to get the movie out of the red. “One Battle” lost $100 million theatrically. It did, however, prove valuable in other ways — namely, winning the best picture Oscar.
Moreover, Warner Bros. could withstand the major write-down because it was riding high on a massive year at the box office. The studio had fielded an unprecedented run of profitable hits , including “Sinners,” “A Minecraft Movie,” “Weapons” and “Final Destination: Bloodlines.” In 2025, the company had seven movies that grossed $100 million domestically and commanded 21% of the North American box office.
Fast forward a year, and Warner Bros. isn’t in the same shape. The studio has yet to release a single film that grossed $100 million domestically, and commands just 6% of the domestic market. That’s while the box office is enjoying its biggest year since the onset of COVID , fueled by the best summer season ever recorded.
For all the eyes on Warner Bros. as the studio braces for new leadership, Paramount isn’t having much better a year. Despite profitable releases like “Scary Movie” and “Scream,” Paramount ranks seventh among studios with just 5% of the domestic marketshare.
Warners is expected to rebound with December’s “Dune: Part III.” The third entry in Denis Villeneuve’s sci-fi franchise, starring Timothée Chalamet, Zendaya and Robert Pattinson, is shaping up to be the highest-grossing installment in the series.
But before returning to the desert planet of Arrakis, the studio has to mop up a lot of red ink. “The Bride!” will lose $100 million theatrically after collapsing with $24 million worldwide against a $90 million budget. “Supergirl” tapped out with $126 million globally against a $170 million budget, and will lose $80 million. “The End of Oak Street,” a sci-fi adventure starring Anne Hathaway and Ewan McGregor, has grossed $121 million worldwide against an $85 million budget, putting estimated theatrical losses between $25 million and $40 million. “Practical Magic 2,” a legacy sequel that brought back Nicole Kidman and Sandra Bullock as witchy sisters, is running out of steam with $92 million globally against a $75 million budget; it could lose around $30 million to $40 million in its theatrical run. (A source close to “Practical Magic 2” disputes the loss and says the film could net a $5 million profit.)
Meanwhile the studio’s few 2026 wins were modest: Emerald Fennell and Margot Robbie’s “Wuthering Heights” adaptation, the studio’s highest-grossing release so far with $242 million worldwide, will generate $40 million in profits. “Lee Cronin’s The Mummy” earned $90 million and will yield around $10 million for the studio. “Mortal Kombat II” grossed $129 million against an $80 million budget and will result in gains of $10 million.

articles.content_orig:
The Braves have performed well against Cristopher Sánchez in the past. It could be the deciding factor.
Yesterday afternoon the Atlanta Braves won a roller coaster of a game as the lead changed four times. Ultimately Austin Riley had his redemption arc and hit the go-ahead three run HR off of Jhoan Duran fastball that was in the triple digits in the eighth inning.
Tyler Mahle , the Braves’ best trade deadline pickup will be taking the mound for the Braves against Cristopher Sánchez. Both pitchers were on completely different trajectories to end the season.
Before he joined the Braves, Mahle had a 5.13 ERA in eighteen starts. Since he joined the Braves he has a 1.99 ERA in nine starts, averaging six innings per appearance. In his first eighteen starts, Sánchez had a 2.00 ERA and averaged 6.5 innings per start. Since then, he has a 4.10 ERA while averaging 6.0 innings pitched. If we look at the last month, it is even worse. Sánchez has a 5.12 ERA since the start of September.
This does not mean the Braves will have it easy today. It is a do or die game for the Phillies so if Sánchez starts to struggle, it would not be shocking to see a starter come in on short rest to take over. Sánchez is a very good pitcher, in fact he will likely get some Cy Young down votes. However, on paper the matchup looks good. The players on the Braves’ playoff roster have a combined OPS of .759 against him in their careers.
Ronald Acuña has an OPS of 1.000 in sixteen ABs, Ozzie Albies has a .500 average and 1.193 OPS in eighteen ABs, and Austin Riley has a .467 average and 1.104 OPS in fifteen ABs against him. The rest of the team has mostly struggled, so there is some pressure on these three to perform. Michael Harris, fresh off of a three hit night, has struggled to an OPS of .321 in fifteen ABs.
Mahle has not faced the Phillies nearly as much as Sánchez has faced the Braves. However, he did face them in back-to-back starts in early September. In those combined starts he pitched 13.0 innings and only gave up one run on ten hits. He struck out six to only one walk. He was able to induce a whopping twenty-three ground balls in that span. He did have some luck with a BABIP of .220, but the results were great.
On paper, the Braves have the edge today. It is truly going to depend on if Acuña, Albies, and Riley can continue to rake against Sánchez in a period where he is clearly worn down at the end of a long season. Of course, other players stepping up would be nice too. If Mahle can perform like he did against the Phillies already this month and the Braves can get to the bullpen relatively early, they will be in a good spot. The Braves lead MLB in wRC+ in the ninth inning.
If the Braves win today, technically the Phillies miss October baseball this season.

Novak Djokovic records his first victory since Wimbledon, extending his record to 30-0 at the China Open in Beijing, which he has won six times; you can watch the WTA/ATP China Open and ATP 1000 Shanghai Masters live on Sky Sports
Wednesday 30 September 2026 14:50, UK
Novak Djokovic returned to action in Beijing 11 years after his last appearance and extended his incredible record to 30 consecutive wins at the China Open on Wednesday.
Djokovic, a six-time winner in the Chinese capital, received a medical timeout in the second set but did enough to defeat Portugal's Nuno Borges 6-3 7-6 (7-2) and reach the second round.
Next up for Djokovic is home favourite Buyunchaokete Bu , who beat Juan Manuel Cerundolo 6-2 5-7 6-4.
"In the second set he started playing better and I struggled a little bit physically to stay fresh," said Djokovic, who arrived in Beijing having suffered opening-round exits at the US Open and at the ATP Masters 1000 event in Cincinnati.
"When I was serving, I was dominating and going through my games quite comfortably. It was helping getting those first serves in, that high percentages makes my life easier in my service games and I played a great tie-break to close it out in two, so I am very happy about that."
Djokovic, 39, was treated on court by the physio at 3-2 down in the second set, but he didn't appear to be hindered by the issue as he saw out his next two service matches to love and played some of his best tennis of the match.
There was only one break of serve during the match, by Djokovic in Borges' first service game.
Djokovic raced ahead in the tie-break and swiftly racked up four match points, but needed only one as Borges found the net.
"That was a really competitive match by the end of it," Annabel Croft told Sky Sports Tennis .
"Djokovic managed to find a way towards that finishing line and actually his service games became more and more efficient. So much of what we talked about in commentary was the physicality of the match and how uncomfortable Djokovic felt."

articles.title_orig: Trump Had the Chance to Address U.S.-China AI Safety. He Threw Xi a Party Instead. - Carnegie Endowment for International Peace
articles.title_zh: Trump Had the Chance to Address U.S.-China AI Safety. He Threw Xi a Party Instead. - Carnegie Endowment for International Peace
articles.content_orig:
Trump leading a toast during the state dinner for Xi on September 24, 2026.  (Photo by Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images)
The summit may be remembered as a fatal blunder, when Washington, Beijing, and the AI industry collectively chose ceremony over action.
The split screen on AI safety last week—between sobering risk and opulent inaction—could hardly have been more stark. In Washington, President Donald Trump hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping for a state visit, rolling out a red carpet at Joint Base Andrews, offering a tour of his ballroom construction site, and holding a ceremonial tea. On substance, by all accounts , the leaders of the world’s AI superpowers said and did little of consequence. Trump did manage to gather a group of AI and tech CEOs at the White House with Xi—not to negotiate AI guardrails, but for a lavish state dinner.
Trump’s AI titans clinked glasses even as their companies released alarming new data about how little apparent control the industry has over its products. OpenAI announced it had paused training of its “ most capable models ” and would resume only with additional safeguards in place after a model “broke out of its secure testing environment as recently as last weekend and took unauthorized actions on the internet,” according to Fortune . Other OpenAI agents had interacted with U.S. government websites, including those of the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Census Bureau, in unexpected or concerning ways—just a few of the numerous entities the software improperly targeted. Anthropic, meanwhile, reported that its newest model showed “misaligned behavior” at least 1.5 percent of the time, according to Axios, which reported that AI companies are investigating “tens of thousands of incidents in which the models behaved in unexpected, sometimes troubling ways.”
If the leading AI companies are themselves sounding the alarm, why can’t our national leaders act to avoid a disaster? If a more harmful incident occurs—in the United States, China, or anywhere else—before meaningful action to regulate or restrain this technology is in place, last week’s summitry will be remembered as a fatal blunder, when Trump, Xi, and the industry collectively chose ceremony over action.
With China and the United States racing for global tech superiority, nothing is more important than to keep AI systems under human control, with guardrails to ensure safety. Some kind of U.S.-China understanding, even in parallel , could reduce the risk.
Sadly, that was not Trump’s agenda. On September 22, speaking before the United Nations General Assembly, the president rejected efforts to regulate AI, comparing concerns about AI safety to his other favorite “hoaxes,” including climate change and election interference. “The United States also totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control” AI, Trump concluded, adding that “we’re going to encourage it, not rein it in.” Following his meetings with Xi, Trump said he wanted to leave AI “exactly where it is. That is China’s position also.” And although Trump’s team put dramatic restrictions around release of Anthropic’s Fable model this summer, those were quickly lifted . Trump’s recent rhetoric suggests no intent to implement anything other than an ad hoc approach to AI safety.
In advance of the summit, Trump’s team did announce an AI dialogue and a new hotline between the United States and China. But Trump and Xi’s meeting yielded no further details or apparent progress. The hotline may simply be an arrangement between Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and China’s vice premier to pick up their phones in a crisis—the diplomatic equivalent of keeping DMs open—or a more formal effort that, according to WIRED , lacks either approval by Trump or “explicit sign-on from China, which has been noncommittal.” While proposals for such a mechanism exist , what we’ve seen so far falls far short of establishing the communication or risk reduction systems that have been used, for example, to prevent nuclear crises.
On its surface, Xi’s position appears reasonable compared to Trump’s. “We have both the capability and responsibility to develop and manage AI for good and ensure that the development of AI is always under human control and serves the well-being of the people,” Xi said at the White House. But at the moment, China seems content to signal generic openness to dialogue without pushing any specific approach to improve AI safety. Although two more meetings between Trump and Xi are planned this year, breakthroughs seem unlikely, especially given Trump’s suspicion of AI safety and China’s deep distrust of U.S. intentions.
To the rest of the world, watching the leaders of the two AI superpowers—one authoritarian, the other chaotic and self-absorbed—seemingly content to admire the problem has to be particularly alarming. Rogue AI incidents this summer included hacks of Australia’s Medicare website and a German wiki website , and an attempted hack of a Nigerian cryptocurrency firm . At the UN Security Council last week, the best one UN expert could muster was an appeal to common humanity: “A mother in Shanghai wants her sons to grow up in a world where AI improves their lives, not undermines them. A father in Chicago wants his daughters to thrive because of AI, not to suffer its harms. Our hopes and concerns are the same, in every nation.”
It is not hard to imagine a path that could bolster AI safety at home, address concerning national security risks, make use of U.S.-China diplomacy, and further develop global guardrails—because that is precisely the path the United States had begun to chart just a few years ago.
In 2023 and 2024, former president Joe Biden issued an executive order and a national security memorandum outlining principles around “ safe, secure, and trustworthy ” development of AI systems. The Biden administration also initiated diplomacy with China around AI safety that resulted in agreement that both countries would keep a human in the loop in nuclear command and control. This was a milestone that, while frustratingly limited in scope, would benefit both sides and address a meaningful risk. At the UN, ambassador Linda Thomas-Greenfield shepherded the first General Assembly resolution on principles for AI globally. Although extremely modest, the resolution had the advantage of making the U.S. regulatory approach—rather than China’s—the starting point for future international regulation.
To be sure, Biden-era efforts were far from fully fledged and—judging by the speed with which the industry has developed and risks have increased—arguably not nearly ambitious enough. But that agenda did set a regulatory floor that could have scaled along with the industry. Trump’s decision to dismantle the Biden-era framework immediately upon taking office, along with his rhetoric this week doubling down on that approach, now looks like something even industry itself—and indeed the world—would like to see reversed.

articles.title_orig: UK research funded by China front company being sent to Beijing's spies, MI5 warns
articles.title_zh: UK research funded by China front company being sent to Beijing's spies, MI5 warns
articles.content_orig:
More than 100 academics linked to British institutions have unwittingly assisted China's espionage operations against the UK via a front company working for its intelligence and security services, MI5 has warned.
In the highly unusual public alert, the UK's internal security service warned universities and academics that continuing ties with China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI) could ultimately lead to criminal charges for aiding a foreign state.
Security minister Dan Jarvis said MI5's warning exposed attempts by Chinese intelligence agencies to use British academic research to undermine UK national security.
He said he had now written to all university vice-chancellors to end relationships with the organisation.
In June, MI5 and its closest partners in the US, Canada, Australia and New Zealand, issued a joint warning that China's military intelligence services were targeting professional networking sites and online job platforms.
This new UK-specific alert goes further, revealing what the service says is a threat that has been growing within British academic institutions.
MI5 says that the CGTRI, sometimes translated as the China Academy of General Technology (CAGT), has "very strong ties" to the Chinese Ministry of State Security (MSS).
"MI5 has identified that the primary purpose of CGTRI is to fund academic research that directly improves MSS technical capability for espionage," it says.
"More than 100 UK-linked academics have contributed to projects funded by MSS via CGTRI," adding that in some cases the researches would not be aware of the front company's role in their project.
UK academics have contributed to CGTRI-funded projects on topics including AI, cyber-security, covert communications systems and steganography, which means hiding a secret message or file inside an ordinary message or object.
"This activity supports Ministry of State Security espionage, which poses a threat to UK national security," MI5 said.
The security alert said that many academic institutions and individuals will have engaged with the CGTRI "in good faith" because the link back to Chinese state security had been "obfuscated".
It continued: "UK academic institutions are strongly advised to immediately review any ongoing or planned collaboration with CGTRI. This is to ensure MSS derives no further benefit from UK universities or research institutions."
The public alert raises the prospect that British academics who do not act on it immediately could ultimately fall foul of the law.
It stressed that the National Security Act, a key piece of legislation passed in 2023 to counter state espionage, created a new offence of assisting a foreign intelligence service where the individual ought to reasonably have known what they were doing so.
Jarvis said: "This alert exposes attempts by Chinese intelligence to covertly benefit from the expertise and research of our academics, undermining our national security, and that of our allies."

articles.title_orig: Iran says it got a U.S. response to its peace proposal as its currency hits a new record low seven months into the war
articles.title_zh: Iran says it got a U.S. response to its peace proposal as its currency hits a new record low seven months into the war
articles.content_orig:
Iranian officials indicated Wednesday they have received an official U.S. response to Tehran’s latest proposal to end the seven-month war , which U.S. President Donald Trump had publicly rejected just days earlier.
The officials did not say what the response contained, and whether it was a rejection or not.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi presented the U.S. response to President Masoud Pezeshkian at a Cabinet meeting, government spokesperson Fatemeh Mohajerani told the state-run IRNA news agency.
“We will make every effort to bring the agreement to fruition and will firmly stand up for the rights of the Iranian people,” Pezeshkian said. “The agreement must now be based on a win-win strategy.”
The Cabinet meeting follows Araghchi’s return to Iran after travelling to New York for the U.N. General Assembly last week. While there, officials held indirect talks with U.S. officials and also met with Qatari and Pakistani mediators on the sidelines of the annual gathering of world leaders.
Araghchi briefed the Cabinet on his trip to New York and the meetings he held there, including Iran’s conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz , which Mohajerani said had been conveyed through mediators.
Araghchi last week said he floated the proposal to reopen the strait in a week if the U.S. agreed to lift its blockade of Iranian ports, release frozen Iranian assets and waive sanctions on Iranian oil sales, among other conditions.
Trump swiftly rejected the proposal , saying Iran wanted to make a deal because it was “losing so badly” but that its offer “would not be acceptable.”
Despite Trump’s public rebuffing, mediators continued working with Iran and the United States on trying to broker a deal to end the fighting and open the strait, according to officials who were not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity.
Meanwhile, the Trump administration says it is is pushing forward with economic warfare against Tehran as the prospects of the two sides coming to an agreement appears uncertain.
The U.S. Treasury Department unveiled new sanctions on Tuesday targeting people and companies around the globe that it accuses of being financial facilitators or enablers of Iran’s military supply chain.
The latest action by the U.S. administration is part of the administration’s “Operation Economic Outcast” campaign, aimed at severing “critical financial lifelines” for the already heavily sanctioned Iranian government.
Ten individuals and entities based in Iran, Hong Kong and Pakistan now face sanctions over accusations of procuring weapons and weapon components for Iran’s defense ministry as it fights its now seven-month war against the U.S.
Iran’s economy, which was under heavy strain before the war started, has been in a freefall since the conflict began in late February.
The country’s currency fell to a new record low on Tuesday, with traders in Tehran exchanging more than 2.5 million rials to the U.S. dollar in a stark reflection of how the war in the Middle East has steadily eroded the Iranian economy .
The latest decline came just 27 days after the rial hit its previous record low of 2.2 million to the dollar on Sept. 2. The currency has repeatedly reached new lows since the war began in February.
Trump on Tuesday said that Iran is “failing very badly, very badly” and predicted anew that the war will be “over with very, very soon.”
At the onset of the conflict, he had predicted that the war would last just weeks. More recently, Trump said he expects it won’t end until after the Nov. 3 midterm elections in the U.S.
Also on Wednesday, two men were executed in Iran over their role in violence during nationwide anti-government protests in January, the state-run IRNA news agency reported.
Citing the country’s judiciary, IRNA said the men took part in unrest in the northeastern city of Mashhad that left four members of the security forces dead earlier this year. Their death sentences were upheld by Iran’s Supreme Court before being carried out Wednesday morning.
The unrest began Dec. 28 amid anger over Iran’s collapsing currency and worsening economy and quickly spread across the country, with demonstrators increasingly calling for the overthrow of the Islamic Republic. Iranian authorities responded with a deadly crackdown.
Rights groups say thousands were killed and tens of thousands arrested, while Iranian authorities have reported a substantially lower death toll.

The scandal engulfing Cornell University over a woman’s allegations that she was gang-raped at a fraternity house has caused some prospective students to shun the Ivy League school, college advisers warned.
A former student identified as Jane Doe sued Cornell and seven male fraternity members, alleging that she was drugged and sexually assaulted for hours in October 2024 at the Chi Phi fraternity house in Ithaca, New York. No arrests have been made in connection to the case, and the local district attorney has said he is reopening the case in light of the civil suit.
Cornell is under fire for its response to the allegations, and Doe has accused the school of failing to protect her or adequately punish those responsible.
Prominent college advisers told the New York Post that several high school students they work with have scrapped plans to apply to Cornell as a result.
“All seven of the college applicants we work with for 2027 who planned to apply Early Decision to Cornell have decided not to apply at all,” Amanda Uhry, the founder of Manhattan Private Schools Advisors, told the newspaper.
“The parents will not permit them to go after what happened,” Uhry said of the seven prospective college students she is advising. “Nobody’s thinking about [applying to] Cornell anymore.”
College consultant Christopher Rim of Command Education said his clients are “shocked” about how Cornell has handled the incident. His international clients are particularly worried and have asked him whether it’s “how all U.S. schools” handle serious allegations.
“Parents who live halfway around the world just want to know their kids are in a safe environment,” he said. “And that remains to be seen.”
At the time of the alleged assault, Doe was 20 years old and a member of a sorority on campus, according to the 101-page complaint filed September 14 in New York County Supreme Court.
The lawsuit alleges that Doe was intoxicated and visiting a friend at the frat house when two male students pressured her into snorting a substance they claimed was ketamine in October 2024.
Multiple male students arrived at the house throughout the night, and Doe was subjected to an hours-long assault by seven of them, according to the complaint.
The filing details graphic abuse including men snorting lines of ketamine off her body, moving her between rooms and continuing to rape and sexually assault her while she was incapacitated.
Doe reported the incident to the Cornell University Police Department three weeks later, and an internal Title IX investigation began in January 2025. However, Doe’s attorney Thomas Giuffra told The Independent that Cornell’s response was severely lacking.
Out of the seven male students named in the civil filing, two were expelled from the university, according to Doe’s legal team. The other students allegedly involved were said to have received lesser punishments, which reportedly included temporary suspensions, required workshops or essay-writing assignments.
Following the uproar over the case, New York prosecutors are reopening the investigation. Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said his office is weighing whether to bring criminal charges related to the incident, but said the allegations in the civil complaint are “dramatically different” from the woman’s statement to police at the time.
Lawmakers and public figures have condemned the alleged perpetrators and the university, including actors Florence Pugh, Mariska Hargitay, Josh Gad and Hudson Williams.
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said she had “serious questions about Cornell’s campus culture and its systems for prevention, reporting, and response” in a statement. New York Attorney General Letitia James is also reviewing the university’s response to the allegations.
Cornell issued a statement supporting the DA’s decision to reopen the case, and pushed back against allegations that the school “did not impose consequential punishments for those involved.”
“A continuation of the false narrative that there were minimal consequences in this case is irresponsible, will make survivors feel less safe and supported, and will perpetuate the underreporting of sexual assault,” said Kyle Kimble, Cornell’s vice president for university relations.
Attorneys representing the named fraternity members have vigorously denied the claims in the lawsuit.

MI5 issues spy alert to UK universities over Chinese front company stealing research
The security alert issued by MI5 regarding a Chinese state-owned conglomerate accused of conducting espionage in the UK reveals the extent to which British intelligence remains concerned about Beijing’s influence, and risks casting a shadow over UK-China cooperation at a time when the bilateral relationship is enjoying a revival.
The UK’s domestic security service on Wednesday warned researchers and academics to cease work with the China Academy of General Technology (CAGT), an organisation MI5 described as a “significant threat”.
The CAGT, which is also known as the China General Technology Research Institute, is accused of paying UK academics working in sensitive fields such as artificial intelligence and cybersecurity for “research that directly improves MSS technical capability for espionage”. The MSS is China’s Ministry of State Security, its intelligence agency.
China’s approach to intelligence gathering involves hoovering up vast amounts of data, often from unsuspecting individuals who believe they are participating in normal research or consultancy work.
This year the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre warned businesses about Beijing-backed attempts to hack into everyday devices such as wifi routers.
Last year, MI5 issued another China-related security alert , warning parliamentarians about approaches from two LinkedIn profiles thought to be linked to Chinese intelligence.
Wednesday’s alert said academic institutions or researchers should be aware of the 2023 National Security Act , which makes it an offence to engage in conduct that is likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence agency. The warning is likely to send a chill through the UK’s cash-strapped higher education institutions, which have for years turned to China for funding and collaboration opportunities.
The UK is one of the leading countries to partner with China’s higher education sector. In May, China’s education ministry announced 219 new transnational education partnerships, with more than a fifth of the approvals being with British universities. That puts the UK at the top of the list of partner countries, ahead of Russia, France and Italy.
Chinese students are also the largest group of non-EU international students in the UK, generating about £600m a year for the higher education sector.
There has been growing concern in the UK that partnerships with China pose a risk to national security. The 2023 Intelligence and Security Committee report on China said UK academic institutions “provide a rich feeding ground for China to achieve both political influence and economic advantage” and flagged the risk of China “directing or stealing UK academic research”.
In this case, MI5 said that more than 100 academics linked to the UK had contributed to projects funded by the MSS via the front company. The areas of interest were AI, cybersecurity and steganography , the embedding of hidden data in pictures online.
Sam Goodman, the senior policy director at the China Strategic Risks Institute, said UK academics were “between a rock and a hard place” when trying to navigate areas of advanced interest that could be of interest to Chinese intelligence. “There is a lack of a coherent steer from government on something like AI. It isn’t particularly clear on AI at this juncture what levels of collaboration we can have with the Chinese,” Goodman said.
after newsletter promotion
Analysts say the UK should do more to highlight which areas are of potentially dual-use interest to Chinese intelligence and provide more guidance to universities and academics.
“It’s all very well issuing these warnings,” says Charles Parton, a senior fellow at the Royal United Services Institute. “Actually far more important, surely, is a consideration of which technologies can be cooperated with China, and which can’t.” He said naming specific Chinese companies as a risk would not help UK researchers to do due diligence on every potential partnership. “The Chinese are not stupid. If they want to hide the origin of someone, they’ll do it,” Parton said.
Meia Nouwens, a senior fellow at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, said more clarity was needed on the UK side to help guide researchers working in sensitive fields.
Nouwens said: “A problem has been that in the past there hasn’t been a great deal of discussion of what areas of research constitute a national security risk. Without understanding the limits are of what the UK seeks to protect, it is impossible to have a conversation about managing risk.”
The MI5 alert specifically accused the CAGT of being a front for China’s intelligence. But any research institution in China is ultimately controlled by the Chinese Communist party. “Research institutes that are conducting research on areas of strategic interest for China such as technology will have oversight from the party-state,” Nouwens notes.
That does not mean any collaboration with Chinese educational institutions is inherently dangerous, but it does mean UK academics working in sensitive fields will feel increasingly uneasy about working with a country that has financially underpinned the UK’s higher education sector for decades.

articles.title_orig: Caitlin Clark keeps Fever's season alive with fiery, historic performance in Game 2 vs. Aces: 'She was the catalyst'
articles.title_zh: Caitlin Clark keeps Fever's season alive with fiery, historic performance in Game 2 vs. Aces: 'She was the catalyst'
articles.content_orig:
INDIANAPOLIS — The scenes 48 hours and 1,849 miles apart were stark. In the first, a morose Caitlin Clark covered her face with a towel draped over her head, her words sharp and direct in attacking a performance her head coach said humbled them . Two days later, Clark beams amid the bright Gainbridge Fieldhouse lights once more, interjecting when someone mentions her fiery competitiveness.
"You think?" she laughs, eyes alight, praise and talking points ready after a 99-89 win over the Las Vegas Aces in Game 2 of the WNBA playoffs first round on Tuesday night.
Clark will not say how ticked off she was by a Game 1 blowout that put the backs of the championship-aspiring Indiana Fever to the wall. What she will do is point out that she hit three shots in a row after the officiating crew called her for a technical foul less than two minutes into the second quarter.
On a night she said the referees struggled — a claim neither side of the court disagreed with — she said she respected the referees for calling it.
Yes, she said, she definitely deserved it. No, she answers, she didn't do it on purpose. No doubt, though, that it further lit a necessary fire.
"We didn't have the mentality [in Game 1] of coming in, kind of puffing our chests a little bit, and I think tonight we really had that," Clark said after sticking hers out with 27 points, 15 assists and 7 rebounds.
The MVP candidate credited Myisha Hines-Allen for the pregame prompting. In the later minutes of the first quarter, Hines-Allen dusted up with Aces center and Game 1 superstar A'ja Wilson, to which Sophie Cunningham waved her hands up to hear from a raucous home crowd, and Clark slapped her singular championship-winning vet's hands.
"That's what we talked about as a team is like, don't be soft," Clark said. "We kind of beat ourselves in that way."
A minute later, Clark reached in on Wilson and ripped the ball to force a jump ball. With every centimeter of movement, the series wrested from the grasp of Wilson to that of Clark. Now it goes back to Las Vegas tied 1-1, and everyone's season is on the line.
"It's about getting hit, but understanding like, listen, we gotta get back up," Aliyah Boston told Yahoo Sports. "You cannot just lay there."
They called it a bounce-back. The intentionality was as clear as the mood shift. In the locker room, head coach Stephanie White drew up the first play to key open Clark on the perimeter. White told everyone she was going to make it.
"I was just trying not to let everybody down because we were all visualizing that I was going to make it, so I needed to get the night started off right," Clark said.
It officially clocked in at 29 feet, a mere 15 seconds into the contest. An early trademark 3 portends a good night for Clark, and Game 2 didn't disappoint. She drew contact for another three points at the free-throw line, thought an ensuing 27-footer would fall ("it just rolled out," she noted), and used the attention to feed Makayla Timpson and Boston on cuts inside an open paint.
Boston finished through contact around Wilson, nearly pristine in her attack and movements, for 22 points on 15 attempts. Kelsey Mitchell did her work as usual, scoring 26 with a sharp 3 of 4 line from the perimeter. Everyone who played scored. They shot a combined 52.1%.
"We just had a presence about us right from the start of the game," Clark said.
Though the Fever looked to be back in business, the deficit grew to eight by the first quarter's end. Jewell Loyd 's 3-pointer to open the second frame sent it to 11.
The Aces, who have only lost a series to the New York Liberty in the playoffs over the last four years, ran over the Fever in Game 1 with a proper sense of understood urgency and desperation. They knew what to expect, knew how to handle it, and operated accordingly.
White described her team as young in that area before the series began, and they swiftly proved the point. An unraveling began in the second quarter the first time around. When the initial thread began to come apart this time, they didn't let it snowball.
Caitlin Clark (mostly) kept her composure as she willed the Fever to a Game 2 win. (Photo by Brian Spurlock/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)
Composure, Boston said, was paramount. Except, well, you know.
"She's just a passionate player," Boston said, laughing at hearing that White and the coaching staff's focus was keeping Clark calm following the technical.
The whistle of Clark's first postseason tech blew in a nine-point deficit. She knows how many consecutive baskets she hit afterward: three. Not including a missed 3-pointer. Also not included: a feed to Boston in the paint, where they tore through the Aces in the first half to a tune of 30-16.
Another 3 drew the Fever within a possession, eliciting a roar from the crowd and a timeout by the Aces. They fell behind by six when Mitchell, the league's second-highest scorer, took a turn. Her running alley-oop off an Aces turnover and Clark assist gave the Fever a lead.
Clark became the first player in postseason history with at least 10 points and 10 assists in a half, setting the mark for most assists with 11. She had 14 points when the Fever led 48-43 at the half. Combined with Mitchell's 12 and Boston's eight, their big three contributed 70% of the scoring. The Aces' trio of A'ja Wilson (10 points), Chelsea Gray (10) and Jackie Young (7) had 27 of 43 in the first half.
"I mean, a double-double in the first half? Pretty incredible," White said. "The way that she moved the ball and attacked from multiple positions. You always expect her to be able to make shots and to facilitate, but I thought how she managed the game was really good and her defensive energy, I thought, was terrific."
The Fever leveled up the Aces in the physicality department, suffocating Wilson into attempting zero field goals in the third quarter. She finished with 22 points, largely rendered ineffective. Jackie Young brought the Aces back into it with a 31-point performance that wasn't enough to make up for 10 points by Gray, and single digits elsewhere.
Clark, meanwhile, shone — though the drawback of such fiery, un-soft approach did rear its head. She fouled out with 2:45 to go when she stepped into the block, attempting to stop a solo Wilson from an easy bucket.
The Fever challenged to no avail. A nervousness settled around the crowd, unsure if losing their attack-mode superstar would unspool a 92-83 lead. Mitchell lay in her trademark finger-roll, Boston drove in. Lexie Hull rebounded two key Aces misses, and Cunningham hit two free throws.
Clark said she intends to "keep my head a little bit more" in the next game, aware that one point could be the difference. The Fever need her on the floor, and at her best.
"She was the catalyst for us here tonight," White said. "And I think she's going to just take it to another level when we go to Game 3."
The fire has to travel. Or else the scene reverses itself again.

articles.title_orig: WhatsApp introduces optional parental controls for teenagers
articles.title_zh: WhatsApp introduces optional parental controls for teenagers
articles.content_orig:
WhatsApp is introducing new parental controls for teenagers, as tech companies continue to come under pressure to provide more age-appropriate experiences for children.
The social messaging app's new tools will give parents a range of options, such as being told when their child joins or leaves a group. It will also let them decide on privacy settings for their account.
In a blog post, WhatsApp, clarified parents would not be given the power to see the messages their teen is sending and receiving, which along with calls would stay private and protected by end-to-end encryption.
And it said the controls were optional, which social media analyst Matt Navarra called an "obvious weakness".
He said the move was "fairly convenient" for Meta, which owns WhatsApp, because it reduced the company's reliance on age verification by putting some responsibility on parents and teenagers.
"Meta is trying to show regulators we have a child safety system, we have parental controls and we're rolling it out across our platforms," he said.
"I think the big unanswered question is whether enough families will actually use it."
The minimum age to use WhatsApp is 13 in the UK, although it is higher in some countries.
According to the firm, parents will be able to adjust or switch off the controls at any time.
The settings will be "straightforward to set up" using a Pin set by a parent, which teens will need if they want to switch off the controls.
Some of the new privacy tools include selecting who can see a child's profile photo and who can add them to groups.
Parents can also choose how their teenager uses Channels, which allows organisations and public figures to send out content.
And they will have the option of choosing between the default 13+ setting for Meta AI, the app's optional built-in AI assistant, or a stricter "Limited Content" option.
"All of these controls are being designed to support open conversations about how to use WhatsApp between parents and teens, while keeping everyone's personal messages private," the company said.
The changes come as pressure mounts on tech companies from governments and regulators to change the way they operate in order to better protect children using their platforms.
In June, the government announced it plans to ban under-16s from social media platforms, with the restrictions expected to come into force in March 2027.
It said "highly effective age assurance" measures would be used to check the age of those using social media.
WhatsApp is currently excluded from the ban because the government considers it a messaging service.

articles.title_zh: Sussexes condemn 'reckless intrusion' after photographer spotted near Archie and Lilibet's school
articles.content_orig:
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have accused an international photographer of "extraordinary recklessness" for looking into the grounds of the school attended by their children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet.
Two men, both wearing backpacks, were spotted circling the perimeter of the school, with police later identifying one of them as an international press photographer.
A spokesman for Prince Harry and Meghan called it "an unacceptable intrusion into the privacy of children".
Harry, Meghan, and their children returned to the UK last month after living in California for six years.
The BBC understands that the two men were observed by both private security and school staff on Monday morning, stopping at various points and looking into the school grounds, before returning to a van which police later established was a rental vehicle.
One of the men was later identified as photographer for a European press agency.
"The decision by photographers to conduct themselves in this way around a school is extraordinarily reckless," Harry and Meghan's spokesman said.
"There is a world of difference between legitimate media activity and photographers walking the perimeter of a school, stopping to look into the grounds and monitoring children as they go about their day."
The spokesman continued: "Whatever photographs they may have been seeking, this was not only an unacceptable intrusion into the privacy of children; it was an irresponsible and ill-considered way to conduct themselves in the vicinity of a school."
The children began school in the UK at the start of September, but changed after a few days after security concerns were raised about traffic during the school run.
Earlier this month, it emerged that the Sussexes are going to be given a review of their publicly funded security, following their move back.
In August, it was reported that the Sussexes would be moving back to the UK and they are thought to be basing themselves at a private property in the Cotswolds area.
Their surprise announcement reignited questions over the level of their publicly funded security in Britain, a topic that has long been a source of anger for Prince Harry.
It is understood that the committee which oversees royal and VIP security, known as Ravec, is to reconsider Prince Harry and Meghan's level of police protection now that they and their two children are full-time residents rather than visitors.
Ravec will assess any risks they face in their new home and the type of trips taken by the couple and their family, such as regular travel routes and school runs.

Mattel on Wednesday named Roger Lynch as its new CEO and chairman, succeeding Ynon Kreiz.
Lynch, who has been a member of Mattel's board since 2018, will take the reins as chairman on Oct. 2 and CEO by Nov. 2, according to the press release .
Lynch is currently the CEO of Condé Nast, a position he has held since 2019. Mike Perlis will serve as Condé Nast's interim CEO while the board begins it search for Lynch's successor, according to a letter from Lynch.
"I am honored by the Board's confidence in me and couldn't be more excited to lead the incredible team at Mattel," Lynch said in the release. "Throughout my years on the Board, I have admired Mattel's brands, its talented people, and unique culture."
Kreiz will leave Mattel after more than eight years at the helm to take a senior leadership position at another public company.
He has led the toymaker and entertainment company through major transformations, including the release of "Barbie," which became the highest-grossing domestic film release of 2023 .
"It has been a privilege to lead Mattel, with a global team dedicated to its mission and purpose, and I am proud of all we have achieved together," Kreiz said in a statement. "Mattel is in a position of strength, with a world-class brand portfolio, product offering, and global capabilities."
Mattel has been working on bolstering its iconic brands, with Hot Wheels as a notable strength. The company is also attempting break into the digital games space in a bid to match rival Hasbro . It acquired full control of its Mattel163 Mobile Games Studio earlier this year.

articles.content_orig:
Carnegie Mellon University, the prestigious institution based in Pennsylvania, will be opening a campus in Miami following a landmark donation from Citadel founder and CEO Ken Griffin. NBC6’s Julia Bagg reports.
Carnegie Mellon University announced Wednesday that hedge fund CEO Ken Griffin is donating $3 billion , with the bulk of the money for a new campus in Miami focused on societal challenges.
The Pittsburgh-based private research university said the gift is the largest ever single gift to a U.S. university.
Watch NBC6 free wherever you are
Griffin’s gift includes $2 billion to build a new 35-acre campus in Miami’s Wynwood neighborhood, just north of downtown. The campus is expected to enroll around 3,500 undergraduate, master’s and doctoral students. Construction is scheduled to begin next year.
Griffin, a GOP megadonor who founded the Citadel investment firm, owns a waterfront home in Miami, which is part of a growing metropolitan area whose population tops 6.4 million.
In 2024, he was the featured speaker at a meeting of the Miami-Dade League of Cities. At the time, Griffin told the gathering about his childhood living in Boca Raton , saying, “And it’s taken me a long time, but I finally ended up in the right part of Florida down here in Miami!”
Griffin also said his public school education at Boca Raton High School prepared him well for college at Harvard. He spent years in Chicago building his firm before moving Citadel to South Florida in 2022, and he is bullish on Miami.
“The quality of life here is extraordinary, great restaurants, we have a vibrant cultural scene,” Griffin said, praising Miami’s diversity.
The area already is home to the University of Miami, a private research university; Florida International University, a public research university; and Miami Dade College, which started out as a community college but also offers some four-year degrees. Combined, enrollment at the three schools totals around 135,000. Several smaller private colleges are also based in the area.
Griffin has donated over the years to causes such as medical research, charter schools and other universities through his charitable organization Griffin Catalyst.
In 2023, he donated $25 million to Miami's Nicklaus Children's Hospital, one of the largest single donations in its 72-year history. And the next year, he donated $50 million to fund the expansion of Baptist Health Miami Neuroscience Institute and another $50 million to the Sylvester Comprehensive Cancer Center at the University of Miami.
But Griffin saw room for something new.
“The opportunity to bring Carnegie Mellon to Miami places our city at the heart of humanistic and scientific advancement and amplifies the University’s international reach and impact,” said Griffin, who is joining Carnegie Mellon’s Board of Trustees, in a news release.
Even before the announcement, Carnegie Mellon had growing ties to Florida, a state where conservatives have increased their influence on higher education.
Its computer science department runs a program designed to teach middle school students in Florida and several other states about AI. The university also is involved in a partnership with the Gates Foundation to deploy AI-powered course materials for introductory math classes at Miami Dade College.

Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) revealed to The Independent what was going through her mind as she watched her Republican colleague, Sen. Eric Schmitt’s (R-Mo.), attempt to catch former special counsel Jack Smith in a potential perjurious lie — only to see it all go off the rails and become a viral embarrassment .
Smith, the former special counsel charged with investigating Trump by then-Attorney General Merrick Garland, testified before the Senate Judiciary Committee on Tuesday .
During that time, Schmitt attempted to catch Smith in a lie by proving he had been in Georgia on Feb. 3, 2024 to watch the Atlanta Hawks game against the Golden State Warriors. Schmitt was trying to prove that Smith was in Atlanta at the same time that Fulton County Prosecutor Fani Willis, who had indicted Trump, disclosed her affair with special prosecutor Nathan Wade.
“You will go down as a total dirtbag,” Schmitt declared. But the moment quickly devolved into chaos when Smith said he did not recall and then later realized he had been in College Park, Maryland to watch the University of Iowa Hawkeyes women’s basketball team play the University of Maryland Terrapins. The moment immediately went viral, as did the reaction from Sen. Katie Britt (R-Ala.),who had a shocked, jaw-agape look frozen on her face as the gotcha tables were turned .
“The minute I heard when they said Hawks and when Jack Smith said I never was at an Atlanta game, when you're from the Midwest, the Hawks also mean the Hawkeyes,” Klobuchar told The Independent . She also took exception to Schmitt calling Smith a “dirtbag.”
Klobuchar would later chastise Smith and confirm that the Hawkeyes led by Caitlin Clark played in Maryland and that the Hawkeyes won. The senior senator from Minnesota who is running for governor said she knew immediately how the mishap came to be.
“Because I was just going to ask some questions about January 6 and everything,” the Minnesota Democrat said. “So when I started asking Smith questions, and then he said that he remembered that he was at the Maryland game because Iowa came, I knew immediately what it was, and so that's when I explained that I believed that they were confused, and it was the Hawkeyes.”
Klobuchar’s father was Jim Klobuchar who covered sports for the Minneapolis Star-Tribune and Klobuchar traveled to Iowa frequently when she ran for the Democratic nomination for president in 2020.
“And I think it does show two things: one, don't ask a question unless you know the answer, and when a prosecutor tells you that that never happened, maybe you should start doubting your chart,” Klobuchar said. “The second thing is the whole reason they did this hearing was to distract from what is going on right now.”
Prior to being elected to the Senate, Klobuchar served as the chief prosecutor for Hennepin County.
“I believe this, you know, costs are up, chaos is up, corruption is up, and instead of doing a hearing on health care or on prescription drug prices, they go and decide to do this one,” she said.
“Well, I guess they got their comeuppance.”

The Galaxy SmartTag 3 launches in the US in November for $29.99.
Samsung has announced its third-generation Bluetooth tracker, the Galaxy SmartTag 3. It combines a smaller design and improved battery life with a few new tracking and software features, including cross-OS support intended to make it easier to share tracking information with friends and family.
As revealed by leaks , the SmartTag 3 has adopted a squircle design, similar to the original SmartTag but with one key difference: There’s no cutout for a key ring. That means you’ll have to buy one of Samsung’s protective cases if you want to directly attach the tracker to keys or a carabiner. It has an IP67 rating for protection from the elements.
The new design has benefits though. The SmartTag 3 is 35 percent smaller and 33 percent lighter than the SmartTag 2. It’s 10 percent more power-efficient too, stretching its replaceable CR2032 battery to 550 days of normal use, or 790 days in power-saving mode.
While previous Galaxy SmartTags only worked with Samsung phones, the new generation has been broadened to support iOS too. Samsung doesn’t seem to expect it’s going to win over AirTag owners, but is instead pitching this as a way to share tracking information with friends, family, or dogwalkers for help with finding lost objects or pets. We’ve reached out to Samsung to confirm if other Android phones will be supported too.
New notification alerts can be set to trigger when a SmartTag 3 moves in or out of a set area, movement detection alerts can trigger for smaller shifts, and location history helps you follow a tag’s movements. Tracking is handled by Samsung’s own Galaxy Find Network, rather than Google’s Find Hub , which launched following the release of the SmartTag 2 . Once you’re within 200ft of the tracker, ultra-wideband (UWB) and Bluetooth 6.0 Channel Sounding combine on supported phones for more precise detection.
The SmartTag 3 is launching in black and white, starting in South Korea, where it goes on sale from October 7th. A US release will follow in early November, priced at $29.99 for a single tracker and $99.99 for a four-pack. That’s the same price as the SmartTag 2, and matches Apple’s latest AirTag and Google’s new Pixel Tag .

articles.title_orig: Trump's AI "constitution" crowns day of accelerating ambition
articles.title_zh: Trump's AI "constitution" crowns day of accelerating ambition
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump's freshly inked pact on artificial intelligence contained a glaring spelling error, triggering mockery online.
Signed Tuesday by Trump and the leaders of major tech companies , the "morally binding" pact is designed to put controls on the advancement of AI — which the president renamed " super intelligence " via executive order.
"It's almost like a constitution in a way, and the biggest ​people in the world signed that, and ​I signed it as president, and it really ⁠is a form of protection," the 80-year-old president told reporters.
But Trump's Sharpie-scrawled signature came above a conspicuous spelling mistake. Beneath the endorsement, the text read: "President Donald J. Trump, President of the Unites States."
Social media users were quick to pounce on the error.
President Donald Trump's freshly inked pact on artificial intelligence contained a glaring spelling error, triggering mockery online (Getty)
"President of the Unites States," former GOP congressman Justin Amash wrote on X without further comment. Political commentator Brian Krassenstein added: "The jokes write themselves."
A number of commentators highlighted the irony of the spelling error in an agreement seeking to regulate intelligence.
"Misspelling the name of your own country in a document about super intelligence is an impressive feat," one commentator wrote on X.
"If this is Super Intelligence, I'll pass," another user added, while a fifth chimed in: "That's absurd no one caught that typo."
The Independent has contacted the White House for comment.
The pact was signed by the leaders of seven big tech companies, including Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg and Sundar Pichai (Getty Images)
The pact, which Trump said would permit companies to perform "tremendous self-policing," was signed by X's Elon Musk , Meta's Mark Zuckerberg , Google's Sundar Pichai, Anthropic's Dario Amodei, OpenAI's Greg Brockman and Nvidia's Jensen Huang.
It outlines four "layers of controls and audits" that the seven companies should undertake in order to provide for the safe advancement of AI.
These include implementing "robust internal controls to monitor the capabilities and alignment of its models" as well as empowering "an internal team to ensure all of the controls, monitoring and detection are operating as intended."
While polls indicate many Americans are deeply worried about the development of AI and some insiders have even said the technology could result in the end of humanity , Trump himself has largely downplayed concerns.
On Tuesday, Trump said that Americans cannot "surrender to fears" about AI, adding: "We can't stifle it."
When asked by a reporter why the public should trust AI firms to regulate themselves, the president replied: "They don't want anything to go wrong…If something goes wrong, their companies are at stake."

China is not expected to materially boost its crude oil imports through the end of the year as oil prices surged above $100 per barrel again and independent refiners struggle to procure cheaper supply amid the near-disappearance of Iranian barrels.
China is on track to import roughly the same volumes of crude oil in September as it did in August, extending the trend of recovering shipments. However, the September-arriving cargoes were bought at oil prices in the $80s before the latest re-escalation in early September sent and kept Brent above $100 per barrel.
China’s crude oil imports rose for the second consecutive month in August as refiners turned to additional non-Middle Eastern supply and boosted overseas fuel shipments amid eased export restrictions.
The August import level was still 23.4% lower compared to the same month last year, but it’s a marked improvement from the June lows of just 7.1 million bpd.
China slashed its total crude oil imports to a decade low in June, culminating three months of very low import levels amid high prices and constrained supply from the Middle East.
September volumes are expected to be more or less around the August levels, but the outlook for the rest of the year has soured as oil is up above $100 per barrel again and the U.S. blockade is effectively eliminating the regular cheap supply on which China’s independent refiners relied for years to remain competitive.
The teapots now could start reducing refinery processing rates as oil prices rise and supply from major exporters such as Venezuela and Iran dries up as a result of U.S. foreign policy decisions.
Chinese state giants are not in a rush to buy much higher volumes of crude at above $100 a barrel with record-high freight costs, either, according to analysts.
“We don’t expect significant upside to China’s crude imports, partly as hefty premiums and expensive freight drive up the cost of feedstock, eroding margins,” Samuel Kong, senior oil analyst at FGE NexantECA, told Bloomberg .
Analysts at FGE NexantECA, as well as at Energy Aspects, have revised down their earlier projections of China’s crude oil imports in the fourth quarter, by about 400,000 barrels per day (bpd). The analysts at these consultancies now expect China’s crude oil imports to be 9.2 million bpd-9.3 million bpd in the fourth quarter, well below last year’s average of 11.6 million bpd.

Prince Harry and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex have condemned what they described as “extraordinarily reckless” behavior by international photographers who they say sparked a security scare at their children’s school.
Private security and school staff are understood to have spotted two young men carrying backpacks, later identified as international photographers, walking around the school and stopping to look into the grounds.
A spokesperson for the Sussexes called the incident on Monday “an extraordinary lack of judgment” and an “unacceptable intrusion” after the photographers were seen “walking the perimeter of the school.”
“It is concerning enough that certain European paparazzi appear unwilling to respect the privacy of children at school,” the spokesperson said. “But to behave in this manner in these particular circumstances, and so soon after the incident at RAF Fairford, demonstrates an extraordinary lack of judgment.”
The spokesperson continued, “Whatever photographs they may have been seeking, this was not only an unacceptable intrusion into the privacy of children; it was an irresponsible and ill-considered way to conduct themselves in the vicinity of a school.”
CNN has reached out to police for comment.
Harry and Meghan switch children’s school just days into term
British media outlets have taken care not to identify the location of the school or the Sussexes’ residence following a request from the Independent Press Standards Organisation, though their rules do not apply to representatives working for international media outlets.
Prince Harry has long expressed concerns over his family’s security, even before they returned to the UK in late August. Earlier this month, they moved Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, from a previous school just days into the start of the academic term due to security practicalities.
When Harry and Meghan stepped back from royal duties in 2020, the British government decided to downgrade their level of taxpayer-funded security – a decision which the duke fought unsuccessfully in the courts for years. In one of those rulings, the UK’s Home Office argued it was not appropriate for wealthy individuals to buy protective security from specialist police officers.
Harry has continued pressing for protection, often drawing comparisons of what his wife has faced with that of his mother, Diana, who died in 1997 in a high-speed car crash while paparazzi were following her.
This latest incident comes as the couple are reportedly waiting on an official risk assessment now they have returned to the UK from Montecito, California.
The couple has been asked to provide authorities with as much detail as possible about their new daily routines, including trips such as the school run, addresses routinely visited, routes taken and more, according to The Telegraph newspaper earlier this month. That information, along with any other evidence considered relevant, will be used by a branch of the UK’s Home Office to evaluate any changes to the level of threat they face.

articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Of all the risks Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) lists in 80-ish pages of warnings, amounting to almost a third of its IPO prospectus, there really is only one: not investing.
That's the resounding message in the aftermath of the Claude maker's IPO documents getting leaked .
The clear implied message of a frontier AI lab on the verge of becoming a $2 trillion company is that investors should join in. Sure, Anthropic listed the risks. But did you notice the expected $2 trillion valuation? Do you want to miss out on that? If the risks truly mattered, the projected valuation would be much closer to zero.
Potential investors will be confronted with the extraordinary message that advanced AI could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity." That's the company's own words via the prospectus, which was reviewed by Reuters. The risks associated with its AI models include "self-preserving behaviors," attempts to "conceal or ‌manipulate information," and behavior "resembling blackmail."
As Reuters notes, Anthropic's IPO risk factors add up to roughly 80 pages of a 261-page document, twice the number of pages the AI lab uses to describe its actual business. SpaceX, which, lest we forget, straps people and cargo onto a controlled explosion and hurls them through the sky into space, used around 38 pages to outline its risk factors.
The financials are just as fraught. Anthropic lost more than $8 billion on an operating basis in 2025, even as revenue grew twelvefold, according to the documents.
But the stark losses, even paired with the existential risks, only underscore just how valuable Anthropic and its backers believe its technology to be. The frontier AI lab views the coming AI era, Reuters reports, as more transformative than industrialization, electricity, and the internet.
The public sale could value the company at more than $2 trillion, leapfrogging almost every major corporation aside from a handful of tech giants, soaking up capital and interest before OpenAI goes to market, and outrunning public warnings about AI's threats to human civilization.
In this light, the dozens of pages of risks look less like formidable liabilities than endearing flaws. Untold future profits outweigh the biggest hypothetical fears.

articles.title_orig: Andy Burnham to fight next election on pledge to change voting system
articles.title_zh: Andy Burnham to fight next election on pledge to change voting system
articles.content_orig:
Andy Burnham has promised that Labour will fight the next general election on a pledge to change the UK's voting system.
In his first party conference speech as prime minister, he announced plans for a national commission to explore options for electoral reform.
He invited other parties to work with the commission to ensure "everyone's vote counts, and everyone's voice is heard".
He has previously supported moves towards a proportional representation (PR) model, telling last year's conference that "PR's time has come".
Westminster's first-past-the-post system, under which candidates with the most votes in each seat are elected, has been called into question as the UK political landscape has fragmented in recent years.
Debate over the system has intensified since Labour amassed a huge parliamentary majority with a 34% vote share in 2024.
Around 100 Labour MPs recently supported a parliamentary amendment in favour of setting up a commission to examine alternative options, a move Burnham himself supported last year when mayor of Greater Manchester.
In his speech Burnham told delegates: "We will all have failed in our public duties if we carry on as we are and open the door of No 10 to a divisive government on less than 30% of the vote or less."
He added: "We can't succeed in the eyes of the world if we continue with the levels of political turbulence we have seen in recent times."
Burnham did not set out details of who would lead his proposed commission, or when it would begin its work.
Any move to change the voting system would be supported by the Liberal Democrats, who had previously urged Burnham to introduce proportional representation before the next election, which must be held by 2029.
However, any move away from first-past-the-post is likely to be resisted by the Conservatives. Reform UK backed introducing PR at the last election, but there has been speculation that its enthusiasm for the move may have since cooled.
Speaking to broadcasters after Burnham's speech, Reform leader Nigel Farage said he was open to debating a potential change to the system "at some point" but other issues were "far more urgent".
He added: "Is this an absolute priority for the general election after the next one? I don't believe that it is."
Support for changing the voting system is also not universal within Labour, with deputy leader Lucy Powell acknowledging that "parts of the Labour Party" are not in favour of it.
Speaking to Politics Live on BBC 2, she said she personally backed electoral reform but declined to specify a proposed new system, adding there were "lots of models" available.
At the last UK election the Liberal Democrats backed the introduction of a single transferable vote (STV) system, which is used for Scottish council elections.
Other options include the additional member system, a hybrid model that combines first-past-the-post with regional party lists that is used to elect members of the Scottish Parliament.
Earlier this year, the Welsh Senedd was elected for the first time using a closed-list proportional representation system .
The Green Party supports electoral reform but Green MP Ellie Chowns said: "The PM cannot acknowledge the unfairness of a system capable of handing power to a government with a minority of the vote share, and then say the answer is to let that happen exactly once more before he fixes it.
"Burnham must act with urgency to immediately jumpstart the National Commission, guarantee timely progress, and ensure its recommendations are delivered in time for a fairer voting system to be in place at the next general election."

articles.title_orig: Parents, teammates of hospitalized ASU hockey player call for coaches to be placed on leave
articles.title_zh: Parents, teammates of hospitalized ASU hockey player call for coaches to be placed on leave
articles.content_orig:
An Arizona State University hockey player remains in the hospital and is "unlikely to recover" after collapsing during an outdoor workout in August. Now, the player's parents and teammates are calling for the university's coaches involved to be placed on leave.
Related video: Which universities spent the most on college football coaches' salaries
ESPN said the parents of Matthew Mayich , 21, released a statement Tuesday through their family attorney, saying he suffered "from exertional heat stroke that reduced the flow of oxygen to his brain" after collapsing during a summer team workout on Aug. 20.
His family said he is unlikely to recover.
The statement comes after seven ASU hockey players sent an anonymous letter to the university's president on Monday, saying Mayich did not receive any water during the workout, which they said was more grueling than reported. They said the athletic staff was not prepared to deal with heat stroke.
The players also noted that Mayich was new to Arizona, having been in the area for only eight days and having been involved in the hockey program for five.
Drafted by the St. Louis Blues, Mayich is from Hamilton, Ontario, according to the NHL .
Players sent the letter anonymously due to fears of retribution from the coaching staff, ESPN said. The players asked for an interim coaching staff to be put in place if the coaches involved are placed on leave.
Arizona State police are investigating the incident. A report will be sent to the Maricopa County Attorney's Office for independent review when completed.
ESPN and the Associated Press contributed to this article.
